entries.d8af4e6dc0bf4c98e84c61189adbd7119738ff1c: <div sID="gen18504" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Ezek.7" sID="Ezek.7"/> <div eID="gen18504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18505" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18506" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the approaching ruin of the land of Israel is most particularly foretold in affecting expressions often repeated, that if possible they might be awakened by repentance to prevent it. The prophet must tell them, I. That it will be a final ruin, a complete utter destruction, which would make an end of them, a miserable end, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.1-Ezek.7.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. That it is an approaching ruin, just at the door, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.7-Ezek.7.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. III. That it is an unavoidable ruin, because they had by sin brought it upon themselves, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.10-Ezek.7.15">ver. 10-15</reference>. IV. That their strength and wealth should be no fence against it, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.16-Ezek.7.19">ver. 16-19</reference>. V. That the temple, which they trusted in, should itself be ruined, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.20-Ezek.7.22">ver. 20-22</reference>. VI. That it should be a universal ruin, the sin that brought it having been universal, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.23-Ezek.7.27">ver. 23-27</reference>.
entries.6cb2eb89d18404c562b1447c10a65b969b3f26d6: <div eID="gen18506" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18505" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Desolation of Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 594.)</title> <div sID="gen18507" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Moreover the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Also, thou son of man, thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> unto the land of Israel; An end, the end is come upon the four corners of the land. <hi type="super">3</hi> Now <hi type="italic">is</hi> the end <hi type="italic">come</hi> upon thee, and I will send mine anger upon thee, and will judge thee according to thy ways, and will recompense upon thee all thine abominations. <hi type="super">4</hi> And mine eye shall not spare thee, neither will I have pity: but I will recompense thy ways upon thee, and thine abominations shall be in the midst of thee: and ye shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">5</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; An evil, an only evil, behold, is come. <hi type="super">6</hi> An end is come, the end is come: it watcheth for thee; behold, it is come. <hi type="super">7</hi> The morning is come unto thee, O thou that dwellest in the land: the time is come, the day of trouble <hi type="italic">is</hi> near, and not the sounding again of the mountains. <hi type="super">8</hi> Now will I shortly pour out my fury upon thee, and accomplish mine anger upon thee: and I will judge thee according to thy ways, and will recompense thee for all thine abominations. <hi type="super">9</hi> And mine eye shall not spare, neither will I have pity: I will recompense thee according to thy ways and thine abominations <hi type="italic">that</hi> are in the midst of thee; and ye shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that smiteth. <hi type="super">10</hi> Behold the day, behold, it is come: the morning is gone forth; the rod hath blossomed, pride hath budded. <hi type="super">11</hi> Violence is risen up into a rod of wickedness: none of them <hi type="italic">shall remain,</hi> nor of their multitude, nor of any of theirs: neither <hi type="italic">shall there be</hi> wailing for them. <hi type="super">12</hi> The time is come, the day draweth near: let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn: for wrath <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon all the multitude thereof. <hi type="super">13</hi> For the seller shall not return to that which is sold, although they were yet alive: for the vision <hi type="italic">is</hi> touching the whole multitude thereof, <hi type="italic">which</hi> shall not return; neither shall any strengthen himself in the iniquity of his life. <hi type="super">14</hi> They have blown the trumpet, even to make all ready; but none goeth to the battle: for my wrath <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon all the multitude thereof. <hi type="super">15</hi> The sword <hi type="italic">is</hi> without, and the pestilence and the famine within: he that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the field shall die with the sword; and he that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the city, famine and pestilence shall devour him. <div eID="gen18507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18508" type="x-p"/> We have here fair warning given of the destruction of the land of Israel, which was now hastening on apace. God, by the prophet, not only sends notice of it, but will have it inculcated in the same expressions, to show that the thing is certain, that it is near, that the prophet is himself affected with it and desires they should be so too, but finds them deaf, and stupid, and unaffected. When the town is on fire men do no seek for fine words and quaint expressions in which to give an account of it, but cry about the streets, with a loud and lamentable voice, "Fire! fire!" So the prophet here proclaims, <hi type="italic">An end! an end! it has come, it has come; behold, it has come. He that hath ears to hear let him hear.</hi> <div eID="gen18508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18509" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">An end has come, the end has come</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.2">v. 2</reference>), and again (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.3">v. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.6">6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Now has the end come upon thee</hi>—the end which all their wickedness had a tendency to, and which God had often told them it would come to at last, when by his prophets he had asked them, <hi type="italic">What will you do in the end hereof?</hi>—the end which all the foregoing judgments had been working towards, as means to bring it about (their ruin shall now be completed)—or <hi type="italic">the end,</hi> that is, the period of their state, the final destruction of their nation, as the deluge was <hi type="italic">the end of all flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.6.13">Gen. vi. 13</reference>. They had flattered themselves with hopes that they should shortly <hi type="italic">see an end</hi> of their troubles. "Yea," says God, "<hi type="italic">An end has come,</hi> but a miserable one, not <hi type="italic">the expected end</hi>" (which is promised to the pious remnant among them, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.11">Jer. xxix. 11</reference>); "<hi type="italic">it is the end, that end</hi> which you have been so often warned of, <hi type="italic">that last end</hi> which Moses wished you to <hi type="italic">consider</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.29">Deut. xxxii. 29</reference>), and which, because <hi type="italic">Jerusalem remembered not, therefore she came down wonderfully,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Lam.1.9">Lam. i. 9</reference>. This end was long in coming, but <hi type="italic">now it has come.</hi> Though the ruin of sinners comes slowly, it comes surely. "<hi type="italic">It has come;</hi> it watches for thee, ready to receive thee." This perhaps looks further, to the last destruction of that nation by the Romans, which that by the Chaldeans was an earnest of; and still further to the final destruction of the world of the ungodly. <hi type="italic">The end of all things is at hand;</hi> and Jerusalem's last end was a type of <hi type="italic">the end of the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.3">Matt. xxiv. 3</reference>. Oh that we could all see that end of time and days very near, and the end of our own time and days much nearer, that we may secure a happy lot <hi type="italic">at the end of the days!</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.12.13">Dan. xii. 13</reference>. This <hi type="italic">end comes upon the four corners of the land.</hi> The ruin, as it shall be final, so it shall be total; no part of the land shall escape; no, not that which lies most remote. Such will the destruction of the world be; all these things shall be dissolved. Such will the destruction of sinners be; none can avoid it. <hi type="italic">Oh that the wickedness of the wicked</hi> might <hi type="italic">come to an end,</hi> before it bring them to <hi type="italic">an end!</hi> <div eID="gen18509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18510" type="x-p"/> II. <hi type="italic">An evil, an only evil, behold, has come,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.5">v. 5</reference>. Sin is <hi type="italic">an evil, an only evil, an evil</hi> that has no good in it; it is the worst of evils. But this is spoken of the evil of trouble; it is <hi type="italic">an evil,</hi> one <hi type="italic">evil,</hi> and that one shall suffice to affect and complete the ruin of the nation; there needs no more to do its business; this one shall <hi type="italic">make an utter end,</hi> affliction needs not <hi type="italic">rise up a second time,</hi> <reference osisRef="Nah.1.9">Nah. i. 9</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">an evil</hi> without precedent or parallel, <hi type="italic">an evil</hi> that stands alone; you cannot produce such another instance. It is to the impenitent <hi type="italic">an evil, an only evil;</hi> it hardens their hearts and irritates their corruptions, whereas there were those to whom it was sanctified by the grace of God and made a means of much good; they were <hi type="italic">sent into Babylon for their good,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.24.5">Jer. xxiv. 5</reference>. The wicked have <hi type="italic">the dregs of that cup</hi> to drink which to the righteous is full of <hi type="italic">mixtures of mercy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.75.8">Ps. lxxv. 8</reference>. The same affliction is to us either a half <hi type="italic">evil</hi> or <hi type="italic">an only evil</hi> according as we conduct ourselves under it and make use of it. But when <hi type="italic">an end, the end, has come</hi> upon the wicked world, then <hi type="italic">an evil, an only evil,</hi> comes upon it, and not till then. The sorest of temporal judgments have their allays, but the torments of the damned are <hi type="italic">an evil, an only evil.</hi> <div eID="gen18510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18511" type="x-p"/> III. <hi type="italic">The time has come,</hi> the set time, for the inflicting of this <hi type="italic">only evil</hi> and the making of this <hi type="italic">full end;</hi> for to all God's purposes <hi type="italic">there is a time,</hi> a proper time, and that prefixed, in which the purpose shall have its accomplishment; particularly the time of reckoning with wicked people, and rendering to them according to their desserts, is fixed, <hi type="italic">the day of the revelation of the righteous judgment of god;</hi> and <hi type="italic">he sees,</hi> whether we see it or no, that <hi type="italic">his day is coming.</hi> This they are here told of again and again (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, the day</hi> that has lingered so long <hi type="italic">has come</hi> at last, <hi type="italic">behold, it has come. The time has come, the day draws near, the day of trouble is near,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.7">v. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.12">12</reference>. Though threatened judgments may be long deferred, yet they shall not be dropped; the time for executing them will come. Though God's patience may put them off, nothing but man's sincere repentance and reformation will put them by. <hi type="italic">The morning has come unto thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.7">v. 7</reference>), and again (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.10">v. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">The morning has gone forth;</hi> the day of trouble dawns, the day of destruction is already begun. <hi type="italic">The morning</hi> discovers that which was hidden; they thought their secret sins would never come to light, but now they will be brought to light. They used to try and execute malefactors in the morning, and such a morning of judgment and execution is now coming upon them, <hi type="italic">a day of trouble</hi> to sinners, <hi type="italic">the year of their visitation.</hi> See how stupid these people were, that, though the day of their destruction was already begun, yet they were not aware of it, but must be thus told of it again and again. <hi type="italic">The day of trouble,</hi> real trouble, <hi type="italic">is near, and not the sounding again of the mountains,</hi> that is, not a mere echo or report of troubles, as they were willing to think it was, nothing but a groundless surmise; as if the <hi type="italic">men that came against them</hi> were but <hi type="italic">the shadow of the mountains</hi> (as Zebul suggested to Gaal, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.36">Matt. ix. 36</reference>) and the intelligence they received were but <hi type="italic">an empty sound,</hi> reverberated from the mountains. No; the trouble is not a fancy, and so you will soon find. <div eID="gen18511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18512" type="x-p"/> IV. All this comes from God's wrath, not allayed, as sometimes it has been, with mixtures of mercy. This is the fountain from which all these calamities flow; and this is <hi type="italic">the wormwood and the gall</hi> in <hi type="italic">the affliction and the misery,</hi> which make it bitter indeed (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will send my anger upon thee.</hi> Observe, God is Lord of his anger; it does not break out but when he pleases, nor fasten upon any but as he directs it and gives it commission. The expression rises higher (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Now will I shortly pour out my fury upon thee</hi> in full vials, <hi type="italic">and accomplish my anger,</hi> all the purposes and all the products of it, <hi type="italic">upon thee.</hi> This wrath does not single out here and there one to be made examples, but it <hi type="italic">is upon all the multitude thereof</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.12">v. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.14">14</reference>); the whole body of the nation has become a <hi type="italic">vessel of wrath, fitted for destruction.</hi> God does sometimes <hi type="italic">in wrath remember mercy,</hi> but now he says, <hi type="italic">My eye shall not spare thee, neither will I have pity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.4">v. 4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.9">again v. 9</reference>. Those shall <hi type="italic">have judgment without mercy</hi> who made light of mercy when it was offered them. <div eID="gen18512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18513" type="x-p"/> V. All this is the just punishment of their sins, and it is what they have by their own folly brought upon themselves. This is much insisted on here, that they might be brought to justify God in all he had brought upon them. God never sends his anger but in wisdom and justice; and therefore it follows, "<hi type="italic">I will judge thee according to thy ways,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.3">v. 3</reference>. I will examine what thy ways have been, compare them with the law, and then deal with thee according to the merit of them, and <hi type="italic">recompense</hi> them to <hi type="italic">thee,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.4">v. 4</reference>. Note, In the heaviest judgments God inflicts upon sinners he does but <hi type="italic">recompense their own ways upon them;</hi> they are beaten with their own rod. And, when God comes to reckon with a sinful people, he will bring every provocation to account: "<hi type="italic">will recompense upon thee all thy abominations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.3">v. 3</reference>); and now <hi type="italic">thy iniquity shall be found to be hateful</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.36.2">Ps. xxxvi. 2</reference>) <hi type="italic">and thy abominations shall be in the midst of thee</hi>" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.4">v. 4</reference>); that is, the secret wickedness shall now be brought to light, and that shall appear to have been in the midst of thee which before was not suspected; and thy sin shall now become an <hi type="italic">abomination</hi> to thyself. So the abomination of iniquity will be when it comes to be an <hi type="italic">abomination of desolation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.15">Matt. xxiv. 15</reference>. Or, <hi type="italic">Thy abominations</hi> (that is, the punishments of them) <hi type="italic">shall be in the midst of thee;</hi> they shall <hi type="italic">reach to thy heart.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Jer.4.18">Jer. iv. 18</reference>. Or therefore <hi type="italic">God will not spare, nor have pity,</hi> because, even when he is <hi type="italic">recompensing their ways</hi> upon them, yet <hi type="italic">in their distress they trespass yet more;</hi> their <hi type="italic">abominations</hi> are still <hi type="italic">in the midst of them,</hi> indulged and harboured in their hearts. It is repeated again (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.8-Ezek.7.9">v. 8, 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will judge thee, I will recompense thee.</hi> Two sins are particularly specified as provoking God to bring these judgments upon them—pride and oppression. 1. God will humble them by his judgments, for they have magnified themselves. <hi type="italic">The rod</hi> of affliction <hi type="italic">has blossomed,</hi> but it was <hi type="italic">pride</hi> that <hi type="italic">budded,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.10">v. 10</reference>. What buds in sin will blossom in some judgment or other. The pride of Judah and Jerusalem appeared among all orders and degrees of men, as buds upon the tree in spring. 2. Their enemies shall deal hardly with them, for they have dealt hardly with one another (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Violence has risen up into a rod of wickedness;</hi> that is, their injuriousness to one another is protected and patronised by the power of the magistrate. The rod of government had become a <hi type="italic">rod of wickedness,</hi> to such a degree of impudence was <hi type="italic">violence risen up. I saw the place of judgment, that wickedness was there,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Eccl. iii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.7">Isa. v. 7</reference>. Whatever are the fruits of God's judgments, it is certain that our sin is the root of them. <div eID="gen18513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18514" type="x-p"/> VI. There is no escape from these judgments nor fence against them, for they shall be universal and shall bear down all before them, without remedy. 1. Death in its various shapes shall ride triumphantly, both in town and in country, both within the city and without it, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.15">v. 15</reference>. Men shall be safe nowhere; for <hi type="italic">he that is in the field shall die by the sword</hi> (every field shall be to them a field of battle) <hi type="italic">and he that is in the city,</hi> though it be a holy city, yet it shall not be his protection, but <hi type="italic">famine and pestilence shall devour him.</hi> Sin had abounded both in city and country, <hi type="italic">Iliacos intra muros peccator et extra—Trojans and Greeks offend alike;</hi> and therefore among both desolations are made. 2. None of those that are marked for death shall escape: There <hi type="italic">shall none of them remain.</hi> None of those proud oppressors that did violence to their poor neighbours with <hi type="italic">the rod of wickedness,</hi> none of them shall be left, but they shall be all swept away by the desolation that is coming (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">None of their multitude,</hi> that is, of the rabble, whom they set on to do mischief, and to countenance them in doing it, to cry, "Crucify, crucify," when they were resolved on the destruction of any, <hi type="italic">none of them shall remain, nor any of theirs;</hi> their families shall all be destroyed, and neither root nor branch left them. This multitude, this mob, divine vengeance will in a particular manner fasten upon; <hi type="italic">for wrath is upon all the multitude thereof</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.12">v. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.14">14</reference>) and <hi type="italic">the vision was touching the whole multitude thereof</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.13">v. 13</reference>), the bulk of the common people. The judgments coming shall carry them away by wholesale, and they shall neither secure themselves nor their masters whose creatures and tools they were. God's judgments, when they come with commission, cannot be overpowered by multitudes. <hi type="italic">Though hand join in hand, yet shall not the wicked go unpunished.</hi> 3. Those that fall shall not be lamented (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">There shall be no wailing for them,</hi> for there shall be none left to bewail them, but such as are hastening apace after them. And the times shall be so bad that men shall rather congratulate than lament the death of their friends, as reckoning those happy that are taken away from seeing these desolations and sharing in them, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.4-Jer.16.5">Jer. xvi. 4, 5</reference>. 4. They shall not be able to make any resistance. The decree has gone forth, and <hi type="italic">the vision</hi> concerning them <hi type="italic">shall not return,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.13">v. 13</reference>. God will not reveal it, and they cannot defeat it; and therefore it <hi type="italic">shall not return re infecta—without having accomplished any thing,</hi> but shall <hi type="italic">accomplish that for which he sends it.</hi> God's word will take place, and then, (1.) Particular persons cannot make their part good against God: No man <hi type="italic">shall strengthen himself in the iniquity of his life;</hi> it will be to no purpose for sinners to set God and his judgments at defiance as they used to do. <hi type="italic">None ever hardened his heart against God and prospered.</hi> Those that strengthen themselves in their wickedness will be found not only to weaken, but to ruin, themselves, <reference osisRef="Ps.52.7">Ps. lii. 7</reference>. (2.) <hi type="italic">The multitude</hi> cannot resist the torrent of these judgments, nor make head against them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">They have blown the trumpet,</hi> to call their soldiers together, and to animate and encourage those whom they have got together, and thus they think <hi type="italic">to make all ready;</hi> but all in vain; none enlist themselves, or those that do have not courage to face the enemy. Note, If God be against us, none can be for us to do us any service. 5. They shall have no hope of the return of their prosperity, with which to support themselves in their adversity; they shall have given up all for gone; and therefore, "<hi type="italic">Let not the buyer rejoice</hi> that he is increasing his estate and has become a purchaser; nor let <hi type="italic">the seller mourn</hi> that he is lessening his estate and has become a bankrupt," <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.12">v. 12</reference>. See the vanity of the things of this world, and how worthless they are—that in a time of trouble, when we have most need of them, we may perhaps make least account of them. Those that have sold are the more easy, having the less to lose, and those that have bought have but increased their own cares and fears. Because <hi type="italic">the fashion of this world passes away,</hi> let <hi type="italic">those that buy be as though they possessed not,</hi> because they know not how soon they may be dispossessed, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.29-1Cor.7.31">1 Cor. vii. 29-31</reference>. It is added (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.13">v. 13</reference>), "<hi type="italic">The seller shall not return,</hi> at the year of jubilee, <hi type="italic">to that which is sold,</hi> according to the law, though he should escape the sword and pestilence, and live till that year comes; for no inheritances shall be enjoyed here till the seventy years be accomplished, and then men shall return to their possessions, shall claim and have their own again." In the belief of this, Jeremiah, about this time, <hi type="italic">bought his uncle's field,</hi> yet, according to the charge, the buyer did not rejoice, but complain, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.25">Jer. xxxii. 25</reference>. 6. God will be glorified in all: "<hi type="italic">You shall know that I am the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">that I am the Lord that smiteth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.9">v. 9</reference>. You look at second causes, and think it is Nebuchadnezzar that smites you, but you shall be made to know he is but the staff: it is the hand of the Lord that smiteth you, and who knows the weight of his hand?" Those who would not know it was the <hi type="italic">Lord that did them good</hi> shall be made to know it is <hi type="italic">the Lord that smiteth</hi> them; for, one way or other, he will be owned.
entries.d8eff04fa0c21a9d610b66390e826ef6d3cc114a: <div eID="gen18514" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Desolation of Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 594.)</title> <div sID="gen18515" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> But they that escape of them shall escape, and shall be on the mountains like doves of the valleys, all of them mourning, every one for his iniquity. <hi type="super">17</hi> All hands shall be feeble, and all knees shall be weak <hi type="italic">as</hi> water. <hi type="super">18</hi> They shall also gird <hi type="italic">themselves</hi> with sackcloth, and horror shall cover them; and shame <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> upon all faces, and baldness upon all their heads. <hi type="super">19</hi> They shall cast their silver in the streets, and their gold shall be removed: their silver and their gold shall not be able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : they shall not satisfy their souls, neither fill their bowels: because it is the stumbling-block of their iniquity. <hi type="super">20</hi> As for the beauty of his ornament, he set it in majesty: but they made the images of their abominations <hi type="italic">and</hi> of their detestable things therein: therefore have I set it far from them. <hi type="super">21</hi> And I will give it into the hands of the strangers for a prey, and to the wicked of the earth for a spoil; and they shall pollute it. <hi type="super">22</hi> My face will I turn also from them, and they shall pollute my secret <hi type="italic">place:</hi> for the robbers shall enter into it, and defile it. <div eID="gen18515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18516" type="x-p"/> We have attended the fate of those that are cut off, and are now to attend the flight of those that have an opportunity of escaping the danger; some of them <hi type="italic">shall escape</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.16">v. 16</reference>), but what the better? As good die once as, in a miserable life, die a thousand deaths, and escape only like Cain to be <hi type="italic">fugitives and vagabonds,</hi> and afraid of being slain by every one they meet; so shall these be. <div eID="gen18516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18517" type="x-p"/> I. They shall have no comfort or satisfaction in their own minds, but be in continual anguish and terror; for, wherever they go, they carry about with them guilty consciences, which make them a burden to themselves. 1. They shall be always solitary and under prevailing melancholy; they shall not be in the cities, or places of concourse, but all alone <hi type="italic">upon the mountains,</hi> not caring for society, but shy of it, as being ashamed of the low circumstances to which they are reduced. 2. They shall be always sorrowful. Those have reason to be so that are under the tokens of God's displeasure; and God can make those so that have been most jovial and have set sorrow at defiance. Those that once thought themselves as the lions of the mountains, so daring were they, now become as the <hi type="italic">doves of the valleys,</hi> so timid are they, and so dispirited, ready to <hi type="italic">flee when none pursues</hi> and to tremble at the shaking of a leaf. They are all of them mourning (not with a <hi type="italic">godly sorrow,</hi> but with the <hi type="italic">sorrow of the world,</hi> which <hi type="italic">works death), every one for his iniquity,</hi> that is, for those calamities which they now see their iniquity has brought upon them, not only the iniquity of the land, but their own: they shall then be brought to acknowledge what they have each of them contributed to the national guilt. Note, Sooner or later sin will have sorrow of one kind or other; and those that will not repent of their iniquity may justly be left to pine away in it; those that will not mourn for it as it is an offence to God shall be made to mourn for it as it is a shame and ruin to themselves, to <hi type="italic">mourn at the last, when the flesh and the body are consumed, and to say, How have I hated instruction!</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.11-Prov.5.12">Prov. v. 11, 12</reference>. 3. They shall be deprived of all their strength of body and mind (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">All hands shall be feeble,</hi> so that they shall not be able to fight, or defend themselves, and <hi type="italic">all knees shall be weak as water,</hi> so that they shall neither be able to flee nor to stand their ground; they shall feel a universal colliquation: their knees <hi type="italic">shall flow as water,</hi> so that they must fall of course. Note, It is folly for the <hi type="italic">strong man to glory in his strength,</hi> for God can soon weaken it. 4. They shall be deprived of all their hopes and shall abandon themselves to despair (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.18">v. 18</reference>); they shall have nothing to hold up their spirits with; their aspects shall show what are their prospects, all dreadful, for they shall <hi type="italic">gird themselves with sackcloth,</hi> as having no expectation ever to wear better clothing. <hi type="italic">Horror shall cover them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">shame,</hi> and <hi type="italic">baldness,</hi> all the expressions of a desperate sorrow, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.11">Isa. xvii. 11</reference>. Note, Those that will not be kept from sin by fear and shame shall by fear and shame be punished for it; such is the confusion that sin will end in. <div eID="gen18517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18518" type="x-p"/> II. They shall have no benefit from their wealth and riches, but shall be perfectly sick of them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.19">v. 19</reference>. Those that were reduced to this distress were such as had had abundance of <hi type="italic">silver and gold,</hi> money, and plate, and jewels, and other valuable goods, from which they promised themselves a great deal of advantage in times of public trouble. They thought their wealth would be <hi type="italic">their strong city,</hi> that with it they could bribe enemies and buy friends, that it would be the ransom of their lives, that they could never want bread as long as they had money, and that <hi type="italic">money would answer all things;</hi> but see how it proved. 1. Their wealth had been a great temptation to them in the <hi type="italic">day of their prosperity;</hi> they set their affections upon it, and put their confidence in it. By their eager pursuit of it they were drawn into sin, and by their plentiful enjoyment of it they were hardened in sin; and thus it was the stumbling-block of their iniquity; it occasioned their falling into sin and obstructed their return to God. Note, There are many whose wealth is their snare and ruin. The gaining of the world is the losing of their souls; it makes them proud, secure, covetous, oppressive, voluptuous; and that which, if well used, might have been the servant of their piety, being abused, becomes <hi type="italic">the stumbling-block of their iniquity.</hi> 2. It was no relief to them now in the day of their adversity; for, (1.) Their <hi type="italic">gold and silver</hi> could not protect them from the judgments of God. They <hi type="italic">shall not be able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the Lord;</hi> they shall not serve to atone his justice, or turn away his wrath, nor to screen them from the judgments he is bringing upon them. Note, <hi type="italic">Riches profit not in the day of wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.11.4">Prov. xi. 4</reference>. They neither set them so high that God's judgments cannot reach them nor make them so strong that they cannot conquer them. There is a day of wrath coming, when it will appear that men's wealth is utterly unable to deliver them or do them any service. What the better was the rich man for his full barns when his soul was required of him, or that other rich man for his <hi type="italic">purple, and scarlet, and sumptuous fare,</hi> when in hell he could not procure a drop of water to <hi type="italic">cool his tongue?</hi> Money is no defence against the arrests of death, nor any alleviation to the miseries of the damned. (2.) Their <hi type="italic">gold and silver</hi> could not give them any content under their calamities. [1.] They could not fill their bowels; when there was no bread left in the city, none to be had for love or money, their silver and gold could not satisfy their hunger, nor serve to make one meal's meat for them. Note, We could better be without mines of gold than fields of corn; the products of the earth, which may easily be gathered from the surface of it, are much greater blessings to mankind than its treasures, which are with so much difficulty and hazard dug out of its bowels. If God give us daily bread, we have reason to be thankful, and no reason to complain, though silver and gold we have none. [2.] Much less could they satisfy their souls, or yield them any inward comfort. Note, The wealth of this world has not that in it which will answer the desires of the soul, or be any satisfaction to it in a day of distress. <hi type="italic">He that loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver,</hi> much less he that loses it. (3.) Their <hi type="italic">gold and silver shall be thrown into the streets,</hi> either by the hands of the enemy, who shall have more spoil than they care for or can carry away (silver shall be nothing accounted of; they shall <hi type="italic">cast that in the streets;</hi> but the <hi type="italic">gold,</hi> which is more valuable, shall be removed and brought to Babylon); or they themselves shall <hi type="italic">throw away their silver and gold,</hi> because it would be an incumbrance to them and retard their flight, or because it would expose them and be a temptation to the enemy to cut their throats for their money, or in indignation at it, because, after all the care and pains they had taken to scrape it together and hoard it up, they found that it would stand them in no stead, but do them a mischief rather. Note, <hi type="italic">The world passes away, and the lusts thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.2.17">1 John ii. 17</reference>. The time may come when worldly men will be as weary of their wealth as now they are wedded to it, when those will fare best that have least. <div eID="gen18518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18519" type="x-p"/> III. God's temple shall stand them in no stead, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.20-Ezek.7.22">v. 20-22</reference>. This they had prided themselves in, and promised themselves security from (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.4">Jer. vii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.3.11">Mic. iii. 11</reference>); but this confidence of theirs shall fail them. Observe, 1. The great honour God had done to that people in setting up his sanctuary among them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">As for the beauty of his ornament,</hi> that <hi type="italic">holy and beautiful house,</hi> where <hi type="italic">they and their fathers praised God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.11">Isa. lxiv. 11</reference>), which was therefore beautiful because holy (it was called the <hi type="italic">beauty of holiness,</hi> and holiness is the beauty of its ornament; it was also adorned with gold and gifts)—as for this, <hi type="italic">he set it in majesty;</hi> every thing was contrived to make it magnificent, that it might help to make the people of Israel the more illustrious among their neighbours. <hi type="italic">He built his sanctuary like high palaces,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.78.69">Ps. lxxviii. 69</reference>. It was a <hi type="italic">glorious high throne from the beginning,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.17.12">Jer. xvii. 12</reference>. But, 2. Here is the great dishonour they had done to God in profaning his sanctuary; they <hi type="italic">made the images of their</hi> counterfeit deities, which they set up in rivalship with God, and which are here called <hi type="italic">their abominations</hi> and <hi type="italic">their detestable things</hi> (for so they were to God, and so they should have been to them), and these they set up in God's temple, than which a greater affront could not be put upon him. And therefore, 3. It is here threatened that they shall be deprived of the temple, and it shall be no succour to them: <hi type="italic">Therefore have I set it far from them,</hi> that is, sent them far from it, so that it is out of the reach of their services and they are out of the reach of its influences. Note, God's ordinances, and the privileges of a profession of religion, will justly be taken away from those that despise and profane them. Nay, they shall not only be kept at a distance from the temple, but the temple itself shall be involved in the common desolation (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.21">v. 21</reference>); the Chaldeans, who are <hi type="italic">strangers,</hi> and therefore have no veneration for it, who are <hi type="italic">the wicked of the earth,</hi> and therefore have an antipathy to it, shall <hi type="italic">have it for a prey</hi> and for <hi type="italic">a spoil;</hi> all the ornaments and treasures of it shall fall into their hands, who will make no difference between that and other plunder. This was a grief to the saints in Zion, who complained of nothing so much as of that which <hi type="italic">the enemy did wickedly in the sanctuary</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.3">Ps. lxxiv. 3</reference>); but it was the punishment of the sinners in Zion, who, by profaning the temple with <hi type="italic">strange gods,</hi> provoked God to suffer it to be profaned by <hi type="italic">strange nations,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">turn his face from those that did it</hi> as if he had not seen them and their crimes and from those that deprecated it as not regarding them and their prayers. Let the soldiers do as they will; let them <hi type="italic">enter into the secret place,</hi> into the holy of holies, as robbers; let them strip it, let them pollute it; its defence has departed, and then farewell all its glory. Note, Those are unworthy to be honoured with the form of godliness who will not be governed by the power of godliness.
entries.9791ffcc187a58a36d884400bbb45db816b6f368: <div eID="gen18519" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Desolation of Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 594.)</title> <div sID="gen18520" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> Make a chain: for the land is full of bloody crimes, and the city is full of violence. <hi type="super">24</hi> Wherefore I will bring the worst of the heathen, and they shall possess their houses: I will also make the pomp of the strong to cease; and their holy places shall be defiled. <hi type="super">25</hi> Destruction cometh; and they shall seek peace, and <hi type="italic">there shall be</hi> none. <hi type="super">26</hi> Mischief shall come upon mischief, and rumour shall be upon rumour; then shall they seek a vision of the prophet; but the law shall perish from the priest, and counsel from the ancients. <hi type="super">27</hi> The king shall mourn, and the prince shall be clothed with desolation, and the hands of the people of the land shall be troubled: I will do unto them after their way, and according to their deserts will I judge them; and they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen18520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18521" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The prisoner arraigned: <hi type="italic">Make a chain,</hi> in which to drag the criminal to the bar, and set him before the tribunal of divine justice; let him stand in fetters (as a notorious malefactor), stand pinioned to receive his doom. Note, Those that break the bands of God's law <hi type="italic">asunder,</hi> and <hi type="italic">cast away those cords from them,</hi> will find themselves bound and held by the chains of his judgments, which they cannot break nor cast from them. The chain signified the siege of Jerusalem, or the slavery of those that were carried into captivity, or that they were all bound over to the righteous judgment of God, <hi type="italic">reserved in chains.</hi> <div eID="gen18521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18522" type="x-p"/> II. The indictment drawn up against the prisoner: <hi type="italic">The land is full of bloody crimes,</hi> full of <hi type="italic">the judgments of blood</hi> (so the word is), that is, of the guilt of blood which they had shed under colour of justice and by forms of law, with the solemnity of a judgment. The innocent blood which Manasseh shed, probably thus shed, by the <hi type="italic">judgment of the blood,</hi> was the measure-filling sin of Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.4">2 Kings xxiv. 4</reference>. Or, It is full of such crimes as by the law were to be punished with death, <hi type="italic">the judgment of blood.</hi> Idolatry, blasphemy, witchcraft, Sodomy, and the like, were <hi type="italic">bloody crimes,</hi> for which particular sinners were to die; and therefore, when they had become national, there was no remedy but the nation must be cut off. Note, Bloody crimes will be punished with bloody judgments. <hi type="italic">The city,</hi> the city of David, the holy city, that should have been the pattern of righteousness, the protector of it, and the punisher of wrong, <hi type="italic">is now full of violence;</hi> the rulers of that city, having greater power and reputation, are greater oppressors than any others. This was sadly to be lamented. <hi type="italic">How has the faithful city become a harlot!</hi> <div eID="gen18522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18523" type="x-p"/> III. Judgment given upon this indictment. God will reckon with them not only for the profaning of his sanctuary, but for the perverting of justice between man and man; for, as <hi type="italic">holiness becomes his house,</hi> so the <hi type="italic">righteous Lord loves righteousness</hi> and is the avenger of unrighteousness. Now the judgment given is, 1. That since they had walked in the way of the heathen, and done worse than they, God would <hi type="italic">bring the worst of the heathen upon them</hi> to destroy them and lay them waste, the most barbarous and outrageous, that have the least compassion to mankind and the greatest antipathy to the Jews. Note, Of the heathen some are worse than others, and God sometimes picks out the worst to be a scourge to his own people, because he intends them for the fire when the work is done. 2. That since they had filled their houses with goods unjustly gotten, and used their pomp and power for the crushing and oppressing of the weak, God would give their houses to be possessed and all the furniture of them to be enjoyed by strangers, and <hi type="italic">make the pomp of the strong to cease,</hi> so that their great men should not dazzle the eyes of the weak-sighted with their pomp, nor with their might at any time prevail against right, as they had done. 3. That, since they had <hi type="italic">defiled the holy places</hi> with their idolatries, God would defile them with his judgments, since they had set up the images of other gods in the temple, God would remove thence the tokens of the presence of their own God. When the holy places are deserted by their God they will soon be defiled by their enemies. 4. Since they had followed one sin with another, God would pursue them with one judgment upon another: "<hi type="italic">Destruction comes, utter destruction</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.25">v. 25</reference>); for there shall come <hi type="italic">mischief upon mischief</hi> to ruin you, and <hi type="italic">rumour upon rumour</hi> to frighten you, like the waves in a storm, one upon the neck of another." Note, Sinners that are marked for ruin shall be prosecuted to it; for God will overcome when he judges. 5. Since they had disappointed God's expectations from them, he would disappoint their expectations from him; for, (1.) They shall not have the <hi type="italic">deliverance out of their troubles</hi> that they expect. They shall <hi type="italic">seek peace;</hi> they shall desire it and pray for it; they shall aim at and expect it: but <hi type="italic">there shall be none;</hi> their attempts both to court their enemies and to conquer them shall be in vain, and their troubles shall grow worse and worse. (2.) They shall not have the direction in the trouble that they expect (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall seek a vision of the prophet,</hi> shall desire, for their support under their troubles, to be assured of a happy issue out of them. They did not desire a vision to reprove them for sin, nor to warn them of danger, but to promise them deliverance. Such messages they longed to hear. But <hi type="italic">the law shall perish from the priest;</hi> he shall have no words either of counsel or comfort to say to them. They would not hear what God had to say to them by ways of conviction, and therefore he has nothing to say to them by way of encouragement. <hi type="italic">Counsel shall perish from the ancients;</hi> the elders of the people, that should advise them what to do in this difficult juncture, shall be infatuated and at their wits' end. It is bad with a people when those that should be their counsellors know not how to consider within themselves, consult with one another, or counsel them. 6. Since they had animated and encouraged one another to sin, God would dispirit and dishearten them all, so that they should not be able to make head against the judgments of God that were breaking in upon them. All orders and degrees of men shall lie down by consent under the load (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">The king,</hi> that should inspire life into them, and <hi type="italic">the prince,</hi> that should lead them onto attack the enemy, <hi type="italic">shall mourn</hi> and be <hi type="italic">clothed with desolation;</hi> their heads and hearts shall fail, their politics and their courage; and then no wonder if <hi type="italic">the hands of the people of the land,</hi> that should fight for them, be <hi type="italic">troubled.</hi> None of the men of might shall <hi type="italic">find their hands.</hi> What can men contrive or do for themselves when God has departed from them and appears against them? All must needs be in <hi type="italic">tears,</hi> all in <hi type="italic">trouble,</hi> when God comes to <hi type="italic">judge them according to their deserts,</hi> and so make then know, to their cost, that he is the Lord, the <hi type="italic">God to whom vengeance belongs.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ezek.7"/> <div eID="gen18523" type="x-p"/>

entries.92f10cc6adc5861a66eecbe218eb1abd352fabb8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11045"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.7.1-Ezek.7.27">Eze 7:1-27</reference>. Lamentation over the Coming Ruin of Israel; the Penitent Reformation of a Remnant; the Chain Symbolizing the Captivity.</title> <div sID="gen19892" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11045"/><hi type="bold">2. An end, the end--</hi>The indefinite "an" expresses the general fact of God bringing His long-suffering towards the whole of Judea to an end; "the," following, marks it as more definitely fixed (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.2">Am 8:2</reference>). <div eID="gen19892" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe8c322fdadf25b78cd77741fee5bb920c5d4027: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11046"/><div sID="gen19893" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11046"/><hi type="bold">4. thine abominations--</hi>the punishment of thine abominations.<div eID="gen19893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall be in the midst of thee--</hi>shall be manifest to all. They and thou shall recognize the fact of thine abominations by thy punishment which shall everywhere befall thee, and that manifestly. <div eID="gen19894" type="x-p"/>
entries.7c38f225ae4f331078a516de21ec9af1d2c359fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11047"/><div sID="gen19895" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11047"/><hi type="bold">5. An evil, an only evil--</hi>a peculiar calamity such as was never before; unparalleled. The abruptness of the style and the repetitions express the agitation of the prophet's mind in foreseeing these calamities. <div eID="gen19895" type="x-p"/>
entries.851db4306cd55a0108fcf47a7bfff197f0c6acf1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11048"/><div sID="gen19896" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11048"/><hi type="bold">6. watcheth for thee--</hi>rather, "waketh for thee." It awakes up from its past slumber against thee (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.65">Psa 78:65</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.66">66</reference>). <div eID="gen19896" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef0c464a9767ca3360cdeda976900ede4eee3a5f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11049"/><div sID="gen19897" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11049"/><hi type="bold">7. The morning--</hi>so Chaldean and Syriac versions (compare <reference osisRef="Joel.2.2">Joe 2:2</reference>). Ezekiel wishes to awaken them from their lethargy, whereby they were promising to themselves an uninterrupted night (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.5-1Thess.5.7">1Th 5:5-7</reference>), as if they were never to be called to account [Calvin]. The expression, "morning," refers to the fact that this was the usual time for magistrates giving sentence against offenders (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.10">Eze 7:10</reference>, below; <reference osisRef="Ps.101.8">Psa 101:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.21.12">Jr 21:12</reference>). Gesenius, less probably, translates, "the order of fate"; thy turn to be punished.<div eID="gen19897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19898" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not the sounding again--</hi>not an empty echo, such as is produced by the reverberation of sounds in "the mountains," but a real cry of tumult is coming [Calvin]. Perhaps it alludes to the joyous cries of the grape-gatherers at vintage on the hills [Grotius], or of the idolaters in their dances on their festivals in honor of their false gods [Tirinus]. Havernick translates, "no brightness." <div eID="gen19898" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5feaca361c7b22e359cc3a9a194579521cc60d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11050"/><div sID="gen19899" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11050"/>8-9. Repetition of <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.3">Eze 7:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.4">4</reference>; sadly expressive of accumulated woes by the monotonous sameness. <div eID="gen19899" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a7e7bc922ee32bac23c8cfe162810598229bf48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11051"/><div sID="gen19900" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11051"/><hi type="bold">10. rod ... blossomed, pride ... budded--</hi>The "rod" is the Chaldean Nebuchadnezzar, the instrument of God's vengeance (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Is 10:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.20">Jr 51:20</reference>). The rod sprouting (as the word ought to be translated), &c., implies that God does not move precipitately, but in successive steps. He as it were has planted the ministers of His vengeance, and leaves them to grow till all is ripe for executing His purpose. "Pride" refers to the insolence of the Babylonian conqueror (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.31">Jr 50:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.32">32</reference>). The parallelism ("pride" answering to "rod") opposes Jerome's view, that "pride" refers to the Jews who despised God's threats; (also Calvin's, "though the rod grew in Chaldea, the root was with the Jews"). The "rod" cannot refer, as Grotius thought, to the tribe of Judah, for it evidently refers to the "smiteth" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.9">Eze 7:9</reference>) as the instrument of smiting. <div eID="gen19900" type="x-p"/>
entries.18eb9b35f5bd62becc95c1b0cea5dd41a6ae0852: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11052"/><div sID="gen19901" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11052"/>11. Violence (that is, the violent foe) is risen up as a rod of (that is, to punish the Jews') wickedness (<reference osisRef="Zech.5.8">Zec 5:8</reference>).<div eID="gen19901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19902" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">theirs--</hi>their possessions, or all that belongs to them, whether children or goods. Grotius translates from a different Hebrew root, "their nobles," literally, "their tumultuous trains" (Margin) which usually escorted the nobles. Thus "nobles" will form a contrast to the general "multitude."<div eID="gen19902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19903" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither ... wailing--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.16.4-Jer.7.25">Jr 16:4-7; 25</reference>:<reference osisRef="Jer.7.33">33</reference>). Gesenius translates, "nor shall there be left any beauty among them." English Version is supported by the old Jewish interpreters. So general shall be the slaughter, none shall be left to mourn the dead. <div eID="gen19903" type="x-p"/>
entries.67c4840428526ce93e78c744f80152fafaf12f22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11053"/><div sID="gen19904" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11053"/><hi type="bold">12. let not ... buyer rejoice--</hi>because he has bought an estate at a bargain price.<div eID="gen19904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor ... seller mourn--</hi>because he has had to sell his land at a sacrifice through poverty. The Chaldeans will be masters of the land, so that neither shall the buyer have any good of his purchase, nor the seller any loss; nor shall the latter (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.13">Eze 7:13</reference>) return to his inheritance at the jubilee year (see <reference osisRef="Lev.25.13">Le 25:13</reference>). Spiritually this holds good now, seeing that "the time is short"; "they that rejoice should be as though they rejoiced not, and they that buy as though they possessed not": Paul (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.30">1Co 7:30</reference>) seems to allude to Ezekiel here. <reference osisRef="Jer.32.15">Jr 32:15</reference>, 37, 43, seems to contradict Ezekiel here. But Ezekiel is speaking of the parents, and of the present; Jeremiah, of the children, and of the future. Jeremiah is addressing believers, that they should hope for a restoration; Ezekiel, the reprobate, who were excluded from hope of deliverance. <div eID="gen19905" type="x-p"/>
entries.db736f64d3bef8f860347d8806333fcc2dbd383a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11054"/><div sID="gen19906" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11054"/><hi type="bold">13. although they were yet alive--</hi>although they should live to the year of jubilee.<div eID="gen19906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19907" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">multitude thereof--</hi>namely, of the Jews.<div eID="gen19907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19908" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which shall not return--</hi>answering to "the seller shall not return"; not only he, but the whole multitude, shall not return. Calvin omits "is" and "which": "the vision touching the whole multitude shall not return" void (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.11">Is 55:11</reference>).<div eID="gen19908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither shall any strengthen himself in the iniquity of his life--</hi>No hardening of one's self in iniquity will avail against God's threat of punishment. Fairbairn translates, "no one by his iniquity shall invigorate his life"; referring to the jubilee, which was regarded as a revivification of the whole commonwealth, when, its disorders being rectified, the body politic sprang up again into renewed life. That for which God thus provided by the institution of the jubilee and which is now to cease through the nation's iniquity, let none think to bring about by his iniquity. <div eID="gen19909" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b04ac6782d90a79baa8f15bf55d8af69f07fdc4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11055"/><div sID="gen19910" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11055"/><hi type="bold">14. They have blown the trumpet--</hi>rather, "Blow the trumpet," or, "Let them blow the trumpet" to collect soldiers as they will, "to make all ready" for encountering the foe, it will be of no avail; none will have the courage to go to the battle (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.6.1">Jr 6:1</reference>), [Calvin]. <div eID="gen19910" type="x-p"/>
entries.a17ed627286baf2a23e6c4385e52082c63652184: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11056"/><div sID="gen19911" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11056"/>15. No security should anywhere be found (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.25">De 32:25</reference>). Fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Lam.1.20">La 1:20</reference>); also at the Roman invasion (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.16-Matt.24.18">Mt 24:16-18</reference>). <div eID="gen19911" type="x-p"/>
entries.c808524357dffd5e98335f424f551835d4ad48f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11057"/><div sID="gen19912" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11057"/>16. (<reference osisRef="Ezek.6.6">Eze 6:6</reference>).<div eID="gen19912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">like doves--</hi>which, though usually frequenting the valleys, mount up to the mountains when fearing the bird-catcher (<reference osisRef="Ps.11.1">Psa 11:1</reference>). So Israel, once dwelling in its peaceful valleys, shall flee from the foe to the mountains, which, as being the scene of its idolatries, were justly to be made the scene of its flight and shame. The plaintive note of the dove (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.11">Is 59:11</reference>) represents the mournful repentance of Israel hereafter (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.10-Zech.12.12">Zec 12:10-12</reference>). <div eID="gen19913" type="x-p"/>
entries.b913187531aa6ddebb68859bb7210d28059582a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11058"/><div sID="gen19914" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11058"/><hi type="bold">17. shall be weak as water--</hi>literally, "shall go (as) waters"; incapable of resistance (<reference osisRef="Josh.7.5">Jos 7:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.14">Psa 22:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.13.7">Is 13:7</reference>). <div eID="gen19914" type="x-p"/>
entries.e82a6ec574804472ccbb69ef2ff8148a6ef8ae57: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11059"/><div sID="gen19915" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11059"/><hi type="bold">18. cover them--</hi>as a garment.<div eID="gen19915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19916" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">baldness--</hi>a sign of mourning (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.24">Is 3:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.37">Jr 48:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.1.16">Mi 1:16</reference>). <div eID="gen19916" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ae48d2376e551cd6e7d4bf30dac019118266c60: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11060"/><div sID="gen19917" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11060"/><hi type="bold">19. cast ... silver in ... streets--</hi>just retribution; they had abused their silver and gold by converting them into idols, "the stumbling-block of their iniquity" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.3">Eze 14:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.4">4</reference>, that is, an occasion of sinning); so these silver and gold idols, so far from "being able to deliver them in the day of the Lord's wrath" (see <reference osisRef="Prov.11.4">Pr 11:4</reference>), shall, in despair, be cast by them into the streets as a prey to the foe, by whom they shall be "removed" (Grotius translates as the Margin, "shall be despised as an unclean thing"); or rather, as suits the parallelism, "shall be put away from them" by the Jews [Calvin]. "They (the silver and gold) shall not satisfy their souls," that is, their cravings of appetite and other needs. <div eID="gen19917" type="x-p"/>
entries.d3dcdf337e10967b67bd3adbbd4b1f4b4a114ffa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11061"/><div sID="gen19918" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11061"/><hi type="bold">20. beauty of his ornament--</hi>the temple of Jehovah, the especial glory of the Jews, as a bride glories in her ornaments (the very imagery used by God as to the temple, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.10">Eze 16:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.11">11</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.21">Eze 24:21</reference>: "My sanctuary, the excellency of your strength, the desire of your eyes."<div eID="gen19918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19919" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">images ... therein--</hi>namely, in the temple (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.3-Ezek.8.17">Eze 8:3-17</reference>).<div eID="gen19919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set it far from them--</hi>God had "set" the temple (their "beauty of ornament") "for His majesty"; but they had set up "abominations therein"; therefore God, in just retribution, "set it far from them," (that is, removed them far from it, or took it away from them [Vatablus]). The Margin translates, "Made it unto them an unclean thing" (compare Margin on <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.19">Eze 7:19</reference>, "removed"); what I designed for their glory they turned to their shame, therefore I will make it turn to their ignominy and ruin. <div eID="gen19920" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f940c75ac97ab74dfcc74a59df4b0e21e4328cb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11062"/><div sID="gen19921" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11062"/><hi type="bold">21. strangers--</hi>barbarous and savage nations. <div eID="gen19921" type="x-p"/>
entries.d2d9899982858b1e6c29da21f504c2ef70cf3a85: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11063"/><div sID="gen19922" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11063"/><hi type="bold">22. pollute my secret place--</hi>just retribution for the Jews' pollution of the temple. "Robbers shall enter and defile" the holy of holies, the place of God's manifested presence, entrance into which was denied even to the Levites and priests and was permitted to the high priest only once a year on the great day of atonement. <div eID="gen19922" type="x-p"/>
entries.3290f3f5e1fa0ec05a459020fbd3913d7bc72087: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11064"/><div sID="gen19923" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11064"/><hi type="bold">23. chain--</hi>symbol of the captivity (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.27.2">Jr 27:2</reference>). As they enchained the land with violence, so shall they be chained themselves. It was customary to lead away captives in a row with a chain passed from the neck of one to the other. Therefore translate as the Hebrew requires, "the chain," namely, that usually employed on such occasions. Calvin explains it, that the Jews should be dragged, whether they would or no, before God's tribunal to be tried as culprits in chains. The next words favor this: "bloody crimes," rather, "judgment of bloods," that is, with blood sheddings deserving the extreme judicial penalty. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.9">Jr 51:9</reference>: "Her judgment reacheth unto heaven." <div eID="gen19923" type="x-p"/>
entries.e33496f6fac31714bf55b1770452a48545a2df44: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11065"/><div sID="gen19924" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11065"/><hi type="bold">24. worst of the heathen--</hi>literally, "wicked of the nations"; the giving up of Israel to their power will convince the Jews that this is a final overthrow.<div eID="gen19924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19925" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pomp of ... strong--</hi>the pride wherewith men "stiff of forehead" despise the prophet.<div eID="gen19925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holy places--</hi>the sacred compartments of the temple (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.35">Psa 68:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.51">Jr 51:51</reference>) [Calvin]. God calls it "their holy places," because they had so defiled it that He regarded it no longer as His. However, as the defilement of the temple has already been mentioned (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.20">Eze 7:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.22">22</reference>), and "their sacred places" are introduced as a new subject, it seems better to understand this of the places dedicated to their idols. As they defiled God's sanctuary, He will defile their self-constituted "sacred places." <div eID="gen19926" type="x-p"/>
entries.87debd65aa75f5559e7edbc1c2ee57ea675ccdd1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11066"/><div sID="gen19927" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11066"/><hi type="bold">25. peace, and ... none--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.3">1Th 5:3</reference>). <div eID="gen19927" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7eb4d2e8dcac8a162f48a83ba1030c8e82d1e77: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11067"/><div sID="gen19928" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11067"/><hi type="bold">26. Mischief ... upon ... mischief--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.32.23">De 32:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.20">Jr 4:20</reference>). This is said because the Jews were apt to fancy, at every abatement of suffering, that their calamities were about to cease; but God will accumulate woe on woe.<div eID="gen19928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19929" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rumour--</hi>of the advance of the foe, and of his cruelty (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.6">Mt 24:6</reference>).<div eID="gen19929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19930" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seek a vision--</hi>to find some way of escape from their difficulties (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.9">Is 26:9</reference>). So Zedekiah consulted Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.17">Jr 37:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.38.14">38:14</reference>).<div eID="gen19930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19931" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">law shall perish--</hi>fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.1">Eze 20:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.74.9">Psa 74:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.9">La 2:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Amos.8.11">Am 8:11</reference>); God will thus set aside the idle boast, "The law shall not perish from the priest" (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.18">Jr 18:18</reference>).<div eID="gen19931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19932" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ancients--</hi>the ecclesiastical rulers of the people. <div eID="gen19932" type="x-p"/>
entries.37eb90c849a4775928676a838ddd21569739407e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11068"/><div sID="gen19933" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11068"/><hi type="bold">27. people of the land--</hi>the general multitude, as distinguished from the "king" and the "prince." The consternation shall pervade all ranks. The king, whose duty it was to animate others and find a remedy for existing evils, shall himself be in the utmost anxiety; a mark of the desperate state of affairs.<div eID="gen19933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19934" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">clothed with desolation--</hi>Clothing is designed to keep off shame; but in this case shame shall be the clothing.<div eID="gen19934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19935" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after their way--</hi>because of their wicked ways.<div eID="gen19935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deserts--</hi>literally, "judgments," that is, what just judgment awards to them; used to imply the exact correspondence of God's judgment with the judicial penalties they had incurred: they oppressed the poor and deprived them of liberty; therefore they shall be oppressed and lose their own liberty. <chapter eID="Ezek.7"/>

entries.72f3440f621b1d14a5145846d2be987d078bae67: <div eID="gen31358" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31359" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31360" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31360" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31359" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31361" type="x-p"/> This chapter, which also forms a distinct prophecy, foretells the dreadful destruction of the land of Israel, or Judah, (for after the captivity of the ten tribes these terms are often used indiscriminately for the Jews in general), on account of the heinous sins of its inhabitants, <reference osisRef="Eze.7.1-Eze.7.15">Eze 7:1-15</reference>; and the great distress of the small remnant that should escape, <reference osisRef="Eze.7.16-Eze.7.19">Eze 7:16-19</reference>. The temple itself, which they had polluted with idolatry, is devoted to destruction, <reference osisRef="Eze.7.20-Eze.7.22">Eze 7:20-22</reference>; and the prophet is directed to make a chain, as a type of that captivity, in which both king and people should be led in bonds to Babylon, <reference osisRef="Eze.7.23-Eze.7.27">Eze 7:23-27</reference>. The whole chapter abounds in bold and beautiful figures, flowing in an easy and forcible language.
entries.ab47e5bf8b03269c86bb5844d913a97d6582cbf8: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen31361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31362" type="x-p"/> An end, the end is come - Instead of קץ בא הקץ kets ba hakkets, one MS. of Kennicott's, one of De Rossi's, and one of my own, read קץ בא בא הקץ kets ba, ba hakkets,"The end cometh, come is the end." This reading is supported by all the ancient Versions, and is undoubtedly genuine. The end Cometh: the termination of the Jewish state is coming, and while I am speaking, it is come. The destruction is at the door. The later hand, who put the vowel points to the ancient MS. that has the above reading, did not put the points to the first בא ba, but struck his pen gently across it, and by a mark in the margin intimated that it should be blotted out. All my ancient MSS. were without the points originally; but they have been added by modern hands, with a different ink; and they have in multitudes of instances corrected, or rather changed, important readings, to make them quadrate with the masora. But the original reading, in almost every case, is discernible. <div eID="gen31362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31363" type="x-p"/> The end is come upon the four corners of the land - This is not a partial calamity; it shall cover and sweep the whole land. The cup of your iniquity is full, and my forbearing is at an end. This whole chapter is poetical.
entries.5783e0b58e1851bae809601f1e1507af91688adb: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen31363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31364" type="x-p"/> Thine abominations shall be in the midst of thee - They shall ever stare thee in the face, upbraid thee with thy ingratitude and disobedience, and be witnesses against thee.
entries.dfe94a4a2cf5265f036fea78b8097a6d55d650d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen31364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31365" type="x-p"/> An evil, an only evil - The great, the sovereign, the last exterminating evil, is come: the sword, the pestilence, the famine, and the captivity. Many MSS. read אחר achar, after. So evil cometh after evil; one instantly succeeds another.
entries.828caef229714367a9a3c7b7f5c009cddbfd8be6: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen31365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31366" type="x-p"/> An end is come, the end is come: it watcheth for thee - This is similar to the second verse; but there is a paronomasia, or play upon letters and words, which is worthy of note. קץ בא בא הקץ הקץ אליך kets ba, ba hakkets, hekits elayich. קצה katsah signifies to make an end or extremity, by cutting off something, and יקץ yakats signifies to awake from sleep: hence קיץ kits, the summer, as the earth and its productions seem then to awake from the sleep of winter. The end or final destruction is here personified; and represented as an executioner who has arisen early from his sleep, and is waiting for his orders to execute judgment upon these offenders. Hence it is said: -
entries.756f21568a7c521d415701e7dbee8ea746e9a39e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen31366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31367" type="x-p"/> The morning is come unto thee - Every note of time is used in order to show the certainty of the thing. The morning that the executioner has watched for is come; the time of that morning, in which it should take place, and the day to which that time, precise hour of that morning, belongs in which judgment shall be executed. All, all is come. <div eID="gen31367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31368" type="x-p"/> And not the sounding again of the mountains - The hostile troops are advancing! Ye hear a sound, a tumultuous noise; do not suppose that this proceeds from festivals upon the mountains; from the joy of harvestmen, or the treaders of the wine-press. It is the noise of those by whom ye and your country are to fall. ולא הד הרים veto hed harim, and not the reverberation of sound, or reflected sound, or reechoing from the mountains. "Now will I shortly pour out," <reference osisRef="Eze.7.8">Eze 7:8</reference>. Here they come!
entries.4b6ea39d27f84d2fa8ea5a6989653ab6b2df0f2b: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen31368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31369" type="x-p"/> Behold the day - The same words are repeated, sometimes varied, and pressed on the attention with new figures and new circumstances, in order to alarm this infatuated people. Look at the day! It is come! <div eID="gen31369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31370" type="x-p"/> The morning is gone forth - It will wait no longer. The rod that is to chastise you hath blossomed; it is quite ready. <div eID="gen31370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31371" type="x-p"/> Pride hath budded - Your insolence, obstinacy, and daring opposition to God have brought forth their proper fruits.
entries.bf761067486416de8a8e56f69b333f187cddac7a: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen31371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31372" type="x-p"/> Violence is risen, up into a rod of wickedness - The prophet continues his metaphor: "Pride has budded." - And what has it brought forth? Violence and iniquity. To meet these, the rod of God cometh. There is such a vast rapidity of succession in the ideas of the prophet that he cannot wait to find language to clothe each. Hence we have broken sentences; and, consequently, obscurity. Something must be supplied to get the sense, and most critics alter words in the text. Houbigant, who rarely acknowledges himself to be puzzled, appears here completely nonplussed. He has given a meaning; it is this: "Violence hath burst forth from the rod; salvation shall not proceed from them, nor from their riches, nor from their turbulence: there shall be no respite for them." Calmet has given no less than five interpretations to this verse. The simple meaning seems to be, that such and so great is their wickedness that it must be punished; and from this punishment, neither their multitude nor struggles shall set them free. They may strive to evade the threatened stroke; but they shall not succeed, nor shall they have any respite. Our Version is to be understood as saying, - None of the people shall be left; all shall be slain, or carried into captivity: nor shall any of theirs, their princes, priests, wives, or children, escape. And so deserved shall their desolation appear, that none shall lament them. This may be as good a sense as any, and it is nearest to the letter.
entries.b2d1eed22452eecdf6ecc51d5593303ee4e0f2d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen31372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31373" type="x-p"/> Let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn - Such is now the state of public affairs, that he who through want has been obliged to sell his inheritance, need not mourn on the account; as of this the enemy would soon have deprived him. And he who has bought it need not rejoice in his bargain, as he shall soon be stripped of his purchase, and either fall by the sword, or be glad to flee for his life.
entries.f06326f62651c865f6e404bf73c29062b0415c1a: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen31373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31374" type="x-p"/> For the seller shall not return - In the sale of all heritages among the Jews, it was always understood that the heritage must return to the family on the year of jubilee, which was every fiftieth year; but in this case the seller should not return to possess it, as it was not likely that he should be alive when the next jubilee should come, and if he were even to live till that time, he could not possess it, as he would then be in captivity. And the reason is particularly given; for the vision - the prophetic declaration of a seventy years' captivity, regards the whole multitude of the people; and it shall not return, i.e., it will be found to be strictly true, without any abatement.
entries.205b6a9c5af7e795e0f112eed2a3d28788b60588: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen31374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31375" type="x-p"/> They have blown the trumpet - Vain are all the efforts you make to collect and arm the peoples and stand on your own defense; for all shall be dispirited, and none go to the battle.
entries.08de8fe0428f06b99119e4df3b1d462a176b6d9f: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen31375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31376" type="x-p"/> The sword is without - War through all the country, and pestilence and famine within the city, shall destroy the whole, except a small remnant. He who endeavors to flee from the one shall fall by the other.
entries.33e0bf798e1270de9e1f5750ce18d90a8a2ff9f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen31376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31377" type="x-p"/> They - shall be on the mountains like doves of the valleys - Rather, like mourning doves הגאיות haggeayoth, chased from their dove-cotes, and separated from their mates.
